meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To those waiting with bated breath for that favourite media catchphrase, the U-turn, I have only one thing to say: You turn if you want to. The lady's not for turning'?
meta.ogDescription: She said it at the 1980 Conservative Party Conference. Ronald Millar wrote it, punning on a 1948 Christopher Fry play Thatcher had not read.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1925–2013 · Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, 1979–1990
answer.sourceLine: Thatcher said it in her speech to the Conservative Party Conference on 10 October 1980 ↗, at the height of the argument over whether she would reverse her economic policy. The words were drafted for her by her speechwriter, the playwright Sir Ronald Millar.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Speech to the Conservative Party Conference
10 October 1980, by Margaret Thatcher as Prime Minister
Sir Ronald Millar (1919–1998), Thatcher’s speechwriter since 1973
A pun on The Lady’s Not for Burning (1948), a play by Christopher Fry

source.excerpt:
But I prefer to believe that certain lessons have been learned from experience, that we are coming, slowly, painfully, to an autumn of understanding. And I hope that it will be followed by a winter of common sense. If it is not, we shall not be diverted from our course.

To those waiting with bated breath for that favourite media catchphrase, the ‘U-turn’, I have only one thing to say: ‘You turn if you want to. The lady’s not for turning!’ I say that not only to you but to our friends overseas and also to those who are not our friends.
trail: The line, the occasion and the date are in Wikiquote’s sourced section for Thatcher ↗, which files it under her 1980 conference speech and notes the Christopher Fry allusion.
Wikipedia’s article on the speech ↗ reproduces the passage verbatim and states that it was written by Sir Ronald Millar as a pun on Fry’s play, “although Thatcher missed the reference herself”.
The same article records that Millar had expected “you turn if you want to” to be the memorable half, and that it was the closing clause which took the headlines.
source.excerptNote: The wording people repeat drops the quotation marks around ‘U-turn’ and the exclamation mark, and stops before the sentence that follows. Wikipedia reproduces the passage in the punctuated form above.

author.name: Margaret Thatcher
author.heading: About Margaret Thatcher
author.bio: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990, the first woman to hold the office and the longest-serving British premier of the twentieth century. Her programme of privatisation, monetarist economics and confrontation with the trade unions was contested at every step, and the 1980 conference speech came at the moment when the pressure to abandon it was greatest. She left office in 1990 after losing the support of her own cabinet.

copyAttribution: "To those waiting with bated breath for that favourite media catchphrase, the ‘U-turn’, I have only one thing to say: ‘You turn if you want to. The lady’s not for turning!’" — Margaret Thatcher, speech to the Conservative Party Conference, 10 October 1980. The words were drafted by her speechwriter Sir Ronald Millar, punning on Christopher Fry’s 1948 play The Lady’s Not for Burning — an allusion Thatcher herself missed.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here: Thatcher really did say it, and the wording is hers to the word. What is routinely wrong is the assumption that she wrote it, and that she was making the literary joke it contains.

items.why: The sentence was written by Sir Ronald Millar ↗, the playwright who had been her speechwriter since 1973. She spoke it; he composed it.
It puns on The Lady’s Not for Burning, Fry’s 1948 verse play. Wikipedia records that Thatcher missed the reference herself ↗ — the allusion was Millar’s, not hers.

misattribution.truthLine: So: genuinely Thatcher’s line to quote, and genuinely Millar’s line to have written ↗. Both facts are usually lost at once.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By the autumn of 1980 unemployment had climbed past two million and Britain was in recession. Thatcher’s own predecessor as Conservative leader, Edward Heath, was among those pressing her to reverse course — to perform the “U-turn” the press kept predicting. The speech was her answer, and it was heard as a refusal to negotiate with circumstance.

The irony sitting inside the most-quoted political sentence of the decade is that its author was a playwright, and its joke was one the speaker did not catch. Millar thought the laugh line was “you turn if you want to”; the conference gave that its own ovation, and then the newspapers took the other half.
detailsBody: The speech as a whole drew a five-minute standing ovation, and the phrase became a shorthand for the whole administration — Charles Moore later titled the first volume of the authorised biography Not For Turning.
context.pull: The most Thatcherite sentence Thatcher ever spoke was written by somebody else.
